Publié le : 07/11/2026 - 04:53 2 min Temps de lecture Le nouveau gouvernement marocain entend faire adopter une réforme de la Moudawana - le Code de la famille - afin d'accompagner l'évolution des moeurs de la société marocaine. Relancée en 2022, assortie de la présentation de plus de 130 amendements au roi Mohammed VI deux ans plus tard : si la question de la Moudawana est revenue sur le devant de la scène depuis plusieurs années maintenant dans le royaume, aucun nouveau texte n'a pour l'instant été voté au Parlement. En cause ? « Les résistances politiques [qui] demeurent importantes » , explique Yassine El Yattioui, docteur en sciences politiques et secrétaire général du Centre marocain de recherche sur la globalisation NejMaroc. « Les questions successorales, le mariage des mineures et la reconnaissance du travail domestique cristallisent les divergences entre sensibilités conservatrices et réformatrices », poursuit ce dernier.

Très encadrée, l'opération, qui ne concernera dans un premier temps qu'une seule province tchadienne, se déroulera en plusieurs étapes. Publié le : 07/11/2026 - 04:53 2 min Temps de lecture Des réfugiés centrafricains dans le camp de Dosseye, dans la province tchadienne du Logone oriental, à la frontière entre le Tchad et la RCA. © Olivier Monodji / RFI Par : RFI Publicité Lire la suite Avec notre correspondante à Ndjamena, Nadia Ben Mahfoudh Alors que près de 147 000 réfugiés centrafricains vivent actuellement au Tchad , Ndjamena, Bangui et le Haut Commissariat des Nations unies pour les réfugiés (HCR) ont signé les modalités pratiques de leur rapatriement volontaire, mercredi 4 novembre, dans la capitale tchadienne. Arrivés par vagues successives depuis le début des années 2000 pour fuir les violences qui ont secoué la Centrafrique , la plupart d'entre eux se sont installés dans quatre provinces du sud du pays où certains camps, notamment autour de Goré, existent depuis près de vingt ans. Parmi ces réfugiés, près de la moitié souhaiteraient désormais rentrer chez eux, selon les enquêtes du HCR qui estime leur nombre à 61 000 personnes environ.

stories.title: Zambia's opposition criticizes government restructuring and layoffs
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5P9Mq Prefer DW on Google Opposition lawmakers have questioned the retirements and dismissals taking place across public institutions Image: Han Xu/Xinhua/picture alliance Advertisement Many people living in Zambia seek careers in the civil service because of the stability and security traditionally associated with government employment. But recent retirements, dismissals and restructuring exercises across several public institutions have unsettled that perception and sparked a national debate about the government's use of "national interest" provisions. Among those affected is former public relations officer Godfrey Chilabi, whose departure from the Zambia Police Service was announced in October. Choosing not to publicly discuss the circumstances surrounding his exit, Chilabi simply told media that he had been retired in the national interest. "Yes, I have been retired in national interest," Chilabi said. "I can't give any reason, but know I'm in retirement." Chilabi's departure came amid a series of changes affecting public institutions in Zambia . Charity Munganga, a Zambia Police Service deputy inspector general, was dismissed, and all staff members at the Zambia Medicines and Medical Supplies Agency were let go as part of a "reset" following a government audit.

Speaking at the National Competitiveness Forum 2026 at Mestil Hotel in Kampala, Minister of State for Finance, Planning and Economic Development (General Duties), Henry Musasizi, said construction plays a central role in supporting growth across agriculture, tourism, manufacturing, mining, technology and housing. He noted that expanding agro-industrialisation requires processing plants, warehouses and cold-chain facilities, while tourism development depends on reliable roads, hotels and accommodation facilities. Public Works Minister Roland Lafayette Giddings disclosed that the measures are contained in new regulations approved by Cabinet to strengthen urban planning, improve sanitation, and address the growing number of abandoned buildings, particularly in central Monrovia. Speaking Tuesday at the Ministry of Information's regular press briefing in Monrovia, Minister Giddings said owners of abandoned properties would be given at least 30 days following official notification to submit plans for rehabilitating their buildings. He warned that failure to comply would attract a monthly fine of US$500, while properties remaining neglected after six months could face demolition or compulsory acquisition, subject to due process and judicial review. The Phase 1b trial, launched by Medicines for Malaria Venture (MMV) in partnership with Rwandan health research organisation Rinda Ubuzima, will assess the safety and tolerability of MMV371, an experimental drug designed to provide extended protection against malaria through a single injection. The injectable could potentially protect recipients for an entire malaria season, reducing the need for frequent preventive medication if its safety and effectiveness are established. The trial marks the first Phase 1 study of a malaria-prevention long-acting injectable to be conducted in Africa and will involve adults and adolescents in Rwanda. The warning follows a wave of social media posts promoting cetirizine - a widely available oral antihistamine used to treat allergies - as a way of tightening the vagina, supposedly to enhance sexual pleasure. Although antihistamines can sometimes cause dryness as a side effect, experts say this does not strengthen vaginal muscles. "Dryness is not tightness... instead, it may increase friction, discomfort, and the risk of tissue injury," the Pharmaceutical Society of Kenya (PSK) said. "Inserting oral tablets is unsafe. stories.title: Can an African feminist have a white wedding? It’s complicated | Patience Akumu
stories.summary: Patience and Mark at their wedding. ‘Getting married as an African feminist felt like the pope renouncing Catholicism – uncomfortable and unlikely.’ Photograph: Courtesy of Patience Akumu View image in fullscreen Patience and Mark at their wedding. ‘Getting married as an African feminist felt like the pope renouncing Catholicism – uncomfortable and unlikely.’ Photograph: Courtesy of Patience Akumu Can an African feminist have a white wedding? It’s complicated Patience Akumu I wanted to be a beacon of black feminist love; my friends and family teased me for being a sellout W e had been together 20 years, had two children and had a customary marriage with our village sub-county two years ago without any real plans for a church wedding. So we called our second ceremony a celebration of love and not a wedding. How else would a self-professed African feminist survive being the centre of a colonial and Abrahamic religious ceremony that also manages to reinforce the most male-centred aspects of African culture? Our invitations came directly from me and my partner Mark, not – as is traditional – from our families, and in the form of a playful gif featuring the song Love Potion from the South African group Mafikizolo, a reminder that this was a wedding on our terms.
